Regarding the definition of "zero-shot generalization" in the context of text-to-image AIs, it seems sensible. The concept of zero-shot generalization refers to the ability of a model to apply its learned knowledge to new, unseen concepts without requiring additional training data. In the context of text-to-image AIs, this means that the model can generate images based on text prompts without having seen the specific images or concepts before.

The 2013 paper that defines zero-shot generalization likely refers to the work of Fei-Fei Li, a computer scientist and director of the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Lab (SAIL). Li has been a prominent researcher in the field of artificial intelligence, particularly in the areas of image recognition and computer vision.

In the context of text-to-image AIs, zero-shot generalization is an important capability, as it enables the model to generate images that are not only relevant to the input text but also novel and creative. This capability has significant applications in areas such as art, design, and entertainment, where the ability to generate new and unexpected images can be highly valuable.

Overall, the definition of zero-shot generalization in the context of text-to-image AIs seems sensible, and it highlights the potential of these models to generate novel and creative images based on text prompts.
